**Y (which feature):**
- In X3-Y1-Z2 and X2-Y1-Z2, only feature 4 fits, so **Y1 = feature 4**.
- In X6-Y3-Z4, only feature 2 fits, so **Y3 = feature 2**.
- In X4-Y4-Z3, only feature 1 fits, so **Y4 = feature 1**. It also fits X5-Y4-Z1.

**X and Z on those features.** Two consistent families explain all six known tasks:

| | Case A | Case B |
|---|---|---|
| X2 | both are 1 | not both are 1 |
| Z2 (true / false) | 3 / 0 | 0 / 3 |
| X3 | at least one is 1 | neither is 1 |
| Z4 (true / false) | 2 / 3 | 3 / 2 |
| X6 | neither is 1 | at least one is 1 |

Both cases fit every example in X3-Y1-Z2, X2-Y1-Z2, X2-Y1-Z4 and X6-Y3-Z4.

**X4 and X5.** In both tasks that use feature 1, the button depends only on whether the two bits differ. So X4 and X5 are "exactly one is 1" and "both are the same", one each. Either order fits:
- If X4 is "exactly one", then Z3 gives 2 when true and 0 when false.
- If X4 is "same", then Z3 gives 0 when true and 2 when false.

No known task links these choices to Case A or Case B, so all four combinations fit.

**What this means for X4-Y4-Z4.** The task compares feature 1 of the two stimuli. The four combinations collapse into two outcomes:
- If the bits differ, the button is 2 and otherwise 3: Case A with X4 = "exactly one", or Case B with X4 = "same".
- If the bits differ, the button is 3 and otherwise 2: the other two combinations.

The data give no reason to prefer either outcome. I chose the first one (bits differ gives 2).

# Learn tasks from examples

Each task maps an input to one of four buttons: 0, 1, 2, or 3. An input is a pair of stimuli; each stimulus has 4 binary features, written as 4 bits (bit positions 1-4, left to right). The line `1011 0110 -> 2` means: stimulus 1 is 1011, stimulus 2 is 0110, and the correct button is 2.

Every task is built from three components. A **Y component** picks one of the 4 features (bit positions 1-4); the task looks at that feature in both stimuli. An **X component** is a rule on those two bits, one of: both are 1; at least one is 1; exactly one is 1; neither is 1; not both are 1; both are the same. A **Z component** gives one button when the rule is true and a different button when it is false. A task's label lists its components, for example X2-Y1-Z3. Each kind has several versions (X1, X2, and so on); different versions of a kind are different from each other, and the same label always means the same component. You are not told which version does what.
